resources.string: How the pleura couples the lungs to the chest wall
A qualitative illustration of normal quiet breathing. Layer thickness, movement and timing are not to scale.
Two layers and a thin fluid film
Parietal pleura lines the inside of the chest wall and covers the upper surface of the diaphragm. Visceral pleura covers the lung. A thin film of fluid lies in the narrow space between them.
During quiet inhalation, the ribs lift and move outward as the diaphragm contracts, flattens and descends. The parietal pleura moves with these surfaces.
The closely apposed pleural layers mechanically couple each lung to the moving chest wall and diaphragm. As the chest expands, the lungs expand with it.
The layers stay close as they glide past each other. The thin fluid film reduces friction; the marks follow the two sheets as the direction of motion reverses.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome again. The ribs settle and elastic recoil reduces lung volume toward its resting level while the pleural layers stay close.
